sections.body:
The sky looks like a big blue blanket over your head. But there is no blanket. The sky is only air, and air is full of things too small to see.

Sunlight looks white to us. That is because white light is really a mix of all the colours. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, and sometimes pink.

When sunlight reaches Earth, it travels through the air. The air is full of tiny particles. Dust, smoke, water, and even the air itself.

Light hits a tiny particle and bounces off it. It bounces in every direction, not just straight ahead. This bouncing is called scattering.

Blue light bounces the most. So blue light reaches your eyes from every part of the sky. Red light mostly goes straight through.

That is the whole secret. The sky is blue because blue light gets scattered around, and your eyes find it everywhere.

The sky is not really blue. It is only blue to your eyes. And the very same rule gives you a red sunset.
examples: The sky is not a blanket. It is just air with tiny bits inside.
Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mix of colours.
Blue light bounces around, so it comes from every part of the sky.
sections.heading: What the sky is really made of

sections.body:
Light travels in straight lines. When it meets a tiny particle in the air, it changes direction. The particle throws a bit of light in many directions at once.

Some colours get thrown much further than others. This is called scattering. Blue and violet light are thrown the most, because their waves are short and bounce around small particles easily.

But we do not see a violet sky. The Sun sends out a little less violet light than blue light, and our eyes are not good at seeing violet. So blue wins.

Look at a cloud and you can see how it works. A cloud looks white because its drops of water scatter all the colours together, and mixing every colour makes white.

Look at the sky near the horizon. It is often pale, almost white. That is because you are looking through more air, so all the colours mix before they reach you.
examples: Blue light bounces around the sky, so it comes from every direction.
Clouds look white because all the colours mix together.
The sky near the horizon is pale, not deep blue.
sections.heading: Why the sky looks blue

sections.body:
When the Sun is high, its light takes a short trip through the air to reach you. When the Sun is low, its light travels a long way to reach your eyes.

On that long trip, blue light gets scattered away. Very little of it arrives. Red and orange light scatter less, so most of it reaches you. That is why a sunset is red.

The same thing happens in the morning. The Sun rises through the same long air, so early light is also warm and orange.

Clouds at sunset catch the red light and glow. This is why the clouds can be pink and purple while the sky behind them is still blue.
examples: At sunset, blue light scatters away, so the sky looks red.
Sunrise is orange for the same reason that sunset is.
The clouds turn pink because they catch the red light.
sections.heading: Why sunsets turn red and orange

sections.body: The Sun is bright enough to hurt your eyes, and your eyes are not built for it. Do not look at the Sun directly, and never through binoculars or a camera without a proper filter. If you want to look at the Sun, watch it near the horizon, where it is softer, and let your eyes look at the sky around it.
sections.heading: Never look straight at the Sun

sections.body:
These four words help you talk about the sky and the light in it.

Sunlight is the light that comes from the Sun. It looks white, but it holds every colour of the rainbow.

A **ray** is one thin path of light. When we talk about a sunbeam, we mean a bundle of rays.

Scattering is the name for light bouncing off tiny particles and spreading out in many directions.

The **atmosphere** is the blanket of air around Earth. It is thin, but it is the layer that makes the sky blue and protects us from too much heat.
examples: The atmosphere is the layer of air around Earth.
Scattering means light bouncing off tiny bits in the air.
That is a ray of light, not a beam of sunshine.
sections.heading: The words we use for the sky

terms.example: Sunlight is white until rain or mist splits it into colours.
terms.gloss: The light that comes from the Sun. It looks white, but it holds all the colours of the rainbow.

terms.example: A ray of light fell right onto my book.
terms.gloss: One thin path of light, like a single beam of sunshine through a gap in the clouds.

terms.example: Scattering is the reason the whole sky is blue.
terms.gloss: When light bounces off tiny bits in the air and spreads out in all directions.

terms.example: The atmosphere is the air around us, going up higher and higher.
terms.gloss: The layer of air around Earth. It is thin, but it scatters the light and keeps us warm.

sections.body:
You do not need any equipment. You only need a good spot and a little patience.

Watch the sky about twenty minutes before the Sun touches the ground. The light changes slowly, so you can see each colour arrive.

Look at the sky on the side the Sun goes down, but do not look at the Sun itself. Then look at the opposite side. That is where you see the Earth's shadow climbing the sky.
examples: The sky turned orange, then pink, then dark blue.
On the other side of the sky there is a dark blue band.
The same colours come back at sunrise, in the other direction.
sections.heading: How to watch a sunset and see the colours change
steps: Find a safe place to sit where you can see the sky.
Start watching about twenty minutes before the Sun goes down.
Notice the white light turn yellow, then orange.
Look at the opposite side of the sky for the Earth's shadow.
Look again the next morning, and watch the colours return.

item.summary: The sky is not blue because of paint or blue water up high. It is blue because sunlight is really a mix of colours, and the tiny bits in the air throw blue light around the whole sky. After reading this you can explain the blue sky, explain a red sunset, and answer the question a friend asks you most often.
item.title: Why Is the Sky Blue?
